# create_html_artifact — one-pager output

## Purpose
This tool exists for exactly one job, and it is a narrow one: producing a static overview or summary of a larger, already-completed body of work, packaged as a shareable one-pager. Good examples of what belongs here: a finished report summarizing findings, a wrap-up of a multi-step task the user just finished with you, a consolidated view of results gathered across a conversation, or a polished recap someone could forward to a colleague without further editing. This is not a general-purpose "make it look nicer" formatter, and it is not a way to make any output feel more finished — most of what you produce in a conversation, including long or well-organized answers, should still just be a normal chat reply.

**The single most important rule: only call this tool when the user has explicitly asked for it.** Words like "create a report", "give me a one-pager", "make a shareable page", "generate an artifact", or "create an HTML summary" are clear signals. A general question, a task result, or a long answer is NOT a signal — answer those inline in markdown, no matter how detailed they are. If the user did not ask for this format, do not use it.

Three additional rules apply once the explicit-request gate is met:
1. Only for an overview or summary of a completed body of work. If the content you're about to generate is itself the primary deliverable — a single answer to a question, one example, one explanation — it does not qualify, even if it's long, even if it's detailed, and even if formatting it as a page would look good. Ask yourself: "is this a recap of work already done, or is this the work itself?" If it's the work itself, this tool is the wrong choice.
2. Static content only, with no exceptions. <script> tags and all inline event handlers are stripped automatically when the artifact is saved, so nothing you produce through this tool can ever actually be interactive, no matter how it's written — buttons won't click, forms won't submit, calculators won't calculate. If the user is asking for something that needs to actually work — an app, a calculator, a live dashboard, anything with real behavior — this tool cannot deliver that and you should use file generation instead, not this tool.
3. Never a substitute for a code snippet or a mermaid diagram, even when the underlying content happens to be HTML or CSS. If what the user actually wants is a code example, a template, a demonstration of how something is built, or a diagram of a flow or architecture, the right home for that is a fenced code block or a mermaid diagram directly in your chat reply — not this tool, even if you could technically wrap that same content in an HTML page.
When you're not sure whether a given request matches this purpose, the safe default is to not call this tool and just reply inline instead. It is far better to under-use this tool than to over-use it.

- Any response where the user did not explicitly request an artifact, report, or one-pager — most answers, summaries, and task results belong in a normal markdown reply.
- Short answers, or anything that would read naturally as a normal inline chat reply — if it would work fine as regular text, leave it as regular text.
- Code snippets, examples, templates, tutorials, or demonstrations of how to build something — this holds true even if the output would technically be a full, well-structured HTML page.
- Diagrams, flows, architecture sketches, or anything that is fundamentally a diagram rather than a document — use a mermaid code block for these instead.
- Anything interactive: forms, calculators, small apps, live dashboards, or any UI element that implies the user will click, type, or interact with it and expect a real response. Remember: this tool cannot produce working interactivity under any circumstances.

## When you do call this tool
- The tool call must be the last action you take in the turn — do not add more content after it. Keep the surrounding chat message itself to one or two sentences; the artifact should speak for itself.
- Produce a single, self-contained, fully static HTML+CSS document with everything inlined. Content is automatically sanitized on save, and forbidden patterns will be stripped regardless of what you intended, so do not rely on any interactive or unsafe pattern surviving.
- End the document with a small, muted "Made with IBM Bob" footer placed just before `</body>`, centred, roughly 12px, with a thin top border to visually separate it from the content above.

---

## Pipeline Overview

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[repo_utils.walk_python_files] -->|.py file paths| B[ast_engine.parse_file_ast]
    B -->|defined_funcs + call tuples| C[graph_builder.build_dependency_graph_from_calls]

    D -->|blast_radius dict| E[main.analyze_repo_target assembles payload]
    E -->|analysis_payload JSON| F[watsonxservice.generate_risk_report]
    F -->|Granite prompt| G[ibm/granite-4-h-small]
    G -->|Markdown report| H[analysis_payload.ai_report]
```

---

## 1. AST Dependency Parser (`ast_engine.py`)

### How the visitor works

[`EnhancedCodeVisitor`](backend/analyser/ast_engine.py:6) subclasses Python's `ast.NodeVisitor`. It maintains two key pieces of mutable state as it walks the AST tree:

| State | Type | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `current_scope` | `List[str]` | A **stack** of class/function names, representing the currently-executing lexical scope |
| `imports` | `Dict[str, str]` | Maps local alias → fully qualified name for all `import` and `from … import` statements |
| `calls` | `List[Tuple[str, str]]` | Accumulated `(caller_fqn, callee_raw)` tuples discovered in the file |

### Scope tracking (the stack)

[`visit_FunctionDef`](backend/analyser/ast_engine.py:32), [`visit_AsyncFunctionDef`](backend/analyser/ast_engine.py:37), and [`visit_ClassDef`](backend/analyser/ast_engine.py:27) all follow the same pattern: push the node's name onto `current_scope`, call `generic_visit` (which descends into children), then **pop** on the way back out. This makes nested functions and methods naturally resolve to paths like `module.ClassName.method_name`.

### Call resolution

[`visit_Call`](backend/analyser/ast_engine.py:42) fires on every call site. It:
1. Assembles the **caller FQN** by joining the module name with the scope stack: `f"{self.current_module}." + ".".join(self.current_scope)`
2. Calls [`_resolve_callee_name`](backend/analyser/ast_engine.py:53), which recursively unwraps `ast.Attribute` chains (e.g. `billing.charge_card` → `"billing.charge_card"`) and `ast.Name` nodes (plain identifiers)
3. Looks up the raw callee in `self.imports` to **dereference aliases** — so `from billing import charge_card` means a call to `charge_card()` resolves to `"billing.charge_card"`
4. Appends the `(caller_fqn, resolved_callee)` tuple to `self.calls`

---

## 2. Multi-Hop Call Graph (`graph_builder.py`)

### Graph construction

[`build_dependency_graph_from_calls`](backend/analyser/graph_builder.py:3) iterates over all `(caller, callee_raw)` pairs collected across every file. For each pair it performs a **fuzzy match** against the full set of known defined functions:

```python
# graph_builder.py:16-18
for full_func in all_defined:
    if full_func == callee_raw or full_func.endswith(f".{callee_raw}"):
        G.add_edge(caller, full_func)
```

The `endswith` check is the cross-module resolution trick: a call recorded as `charge_card` will match a defined function `billing.charge_card`. Each edge in the `nx.DiGraph` is directed **caller → callee**.

### Blast radius traversal (multi-hop)

[`get_blast_radius`](backend/analyser/graph_builder.py:22) uses two NetworkX traversals on the reversed direction — "who calls the target?" means walking **backwards** through the edges (predecessors):

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[cart.checkout_flow] -->|calls| B[checkout.complete_order]
    B -->|calls| C[billing.charge_card]:::target
    classDef target fill:#f66
```

| Hop level | NetworkX call | What it finds |
|---|---|---|
| **Direct (1-hop)** | `graph.predecessors(modified_function)` | Nodes with a direct edge → target |
| **All affected** | `nx.ancestors(graph, modified_function)` | All nodes that can reach target via any path length |
| **Indirect (2+ hops)** | `all_affected - direct_callers` | Everything reachable that isn't a 1-hop caller |

`nx.ancestors` performs a full reverse BFS/DFS under the hood, so arbitrarily deep transitive callers are captured in a single call.

---

## 3. Payload Assembly (`main.py`)

[`analyze_repo_target`](backend/main.py:15) assembles the `analysis_payload` dict that flows into watsonx:

```python
# main.py:36-41
analysis_payload = {
    "target": target_function,       # e.g. "billing.charge_card"
    "nodes": list(graph.nodes()),    # all known function FQNs
    "edges": list(graph.edges()),    # all (caller, callee) directed edges
    "blast_radius": impact           # {"direct": [...], "indirect": [...]}
}
```

Only `target` and `blast_radius` are extracted by [`generate_risk_report`](watsonxservice.py:15) — `nodes` and `edges` travel along but are not sent to the model; they're available for the frontend/API to visualise the full graph.

---

## 4. watsonx Granite Integration (`watsonxservice.py`)

### Credential resolution

[`generate_risk_report`](watsonxservice.py:15) checks for two naming conventions to be environment-flexible:

```python
# watsonxservice.py:25-27
api_key    = os.getenv("WATSONX_APIKEY")    or os.getenv("IBM_API_KEY")
project_id = os.getenv("WATSONX_PROJECT_ID") or os.getenv("IBM_PROJECT_ID")
url        = os.getenv("WATSONX_URL")        or os.getenv("IBM_URL", "https://us-south.ml.cloud.ibm.com")
```

### Prompt structure

The prompt sent to Granite is a tightly constrained instruction-following prompt. It injects the three key variables extracted from the payload — `target`, `direct`, `indirect` — and strictly mandates exactly four Markdown sections, blocking hallucinated sections by name:

```
**Risk Assessment** → risk level + justification
**Impact Summary** → upstream feature breakdown
**Recommended Test Suite** → exact functions/flows to test before merge
**Safety Recommendations** → advice to avoid breaking changes
```

### ModelInference call

The model is invoked via the [`ibm_watsonx_ai` SDK](watsonxservice.py:8) using these generation parameters:

| Parameter | Value | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `DECODING_METHOD` | `"greedy"` | Deterministic, highest-probability token at each step — good for structured output |
| `MAX_NEW_TOKENS` | `450` | Caps response length, keeps it concise |
| `MIN_NEW_TOKENS` | `40` | Prevents trivially short or empty responses |
| `model_id` | `ibm/granite-4-h-small` | IBM Granite 4 small variant for fast inference |

### Fallback mode

If the SDK is not installed **or** credentials are missing, the function short-circuits at [`line 30`](watsonxservice.py:30) and returns a fully-structured Markdown mock report that computes risk severity locally using simple heuristics (`len(direct) + len(indirect) > 2` → HIGH, etc.), so the pipeline always returns a usable result.

---

## End-to-End Data Flow Summary

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant M as main.py
    participant AST as ast_engine
    participant GB as graph_builder
    participant WX as watsonxservice
    participant G as Granite (ibm/granite-4-h-small)

    M->>AST: parse_file_ast(file, module)
    AST-->>M: (defined_funcs, [(caller, callee), ...])
    M->>GB: build_dependency_graph_from_calls(parsed_data)
    GB-->>M: nx.DiGraph (caller→callee edges)
    M->>GB: get_blast_radius(graph, target)
    GB-->>M: {direct: [...], indirect: [...]}
    M->>WX: generate_risk_report(analysis_payload)
    WX->>G: ModelInference.generate_text(prompt)
    G-->>WX: Markdown risk report
    WX-->>M: ai_report string
```

The key design insight is the **separation of concerns**: the AST engine handles syntax-level symbol resolution and alias dereferencing, the graph builder handles topology and multi-hop reachability via `nx.ancestors`, and watsonx only ever sees a clean semantic summary (`target` + two lists) — not raw code or graph edges — keeping the prompt tight and the model output predictable.

The goal is to make the Blast Radius pipeline fully automatic when triggered by a GitHub PR.
Instead of hard-coding a target function name in the workflow, the system should:

1. Fetch the raw git diff for the PR
2. Identify which Python functions were modified using the diff
3. Run the existing AST + graph analysis on those functions
4. Generate an IBM watsonx Granite risk report for each modified function
5. Post the aggregated markdown report as a PR comment

All of the building blocks already exist in the codebase. The work is primarily:
- Writing a new orchestration script (`diff_analyzer.py`) that connects them
- Adding a helper to `cli.py` for diff-driven invocation
- Updating `.github/workflows/blast_radius.yml` to use the new flow

No existing files need to be restructured. `ibm.py` (legacy prototype) is not touched.

---

## Sub-Task 1 — Create `diff_analyzer.py`: Git Diff → Modified Functions

**Status:** [ ] pending

### Intent
Bridge the existing `parse_git_diff()` and `map_line_to_function()` utilities into a single callable that accepts a raw unified diff string and returns a deduplicated list of fully-qualified modified function names (e.g. `["billing.charge_card", "checkout.complete_order"]`).

This is the only genuinely missing piece of logic in the project. Everything it calls already exists.

### Expected Outcomes
- A new top-level file `diff_analyzer.py` with one public function: `get_modified_functions(diff_text, repo_path) -> List[str]`
- Given a diff that touches line 42 of `billing.py`, the function returns `["billing.charge_card"]`
- Files that are not Python, do not exist in the repo, or have no matched function are silently skipped
- The function is importable from `cli.py` and the updated workflow

### Todo List
1. Create `diff_analyzer.py` at the project root
2. Import `parse_git_diff` from `backend.repo_utils` and `map_line_to_function` from `backend.analyser.ast_engine`
3. Implement `get_modified_functions(diff_text, repo_path)`:
   - Call `parse_git_diff(diff_text)` to get a list of `{"file", "added_lines", "removed_lines"}` entries
   - For each entry, skip non-`.py` files
   - Resolve the file path relative to `repo_path` (strip leading `repo_path/` prefix if present)
   - For each added and removed line number, call `map_line_to_function(abs_file_path, line_number)`
   - Collect all non-empty return values into a set (deduplication)
   - Return the set as a sorted list

**Status:** [ ] pending

- `cli.py:15` — `build_markdown_banner(target, blast_radius)` — reuse unchanged for each function

- `diff_analyzer.py` (Sub-Task 1) — `get_modified_functions(diff_text, repo_path)`

Confirm the full pipeline works correctly by running it locally with a manually constructed diff against one of the sample repos. This catches integration issues before a live PR is used.

- `backend/api/test.py` — existing unit tests for `parse_git_diff` and `walk_python_files`; run these after Sub-Task 1 to confirm nothing regressed
